title: What Are Flavonoids in Cannabis? Cannflavins Explained
h1: Cannabis Flavonoids: Color, Chemistry and Cannflavins
metaDescription: Cannabis flavonoids explained: what they do in the plant, the main ones including cannflavins, what lab research shows and how they differ from terpenes.
excerpt: Flavonoids give plants color and protection, and cannabis makes more than 20 of them, including a few found almost nowhere else. Here is what they are and what science can and cannot say yet.
keyTakeaways: Flavonoids are plant polyphenols found in fruits, vegetables, tea and wine, and more than 20 have been identified in cannabis.
In plants they help with color, UV screening and defense against stress, microbes and insects.
Cannflavins A, B and C are almost unique to cannabis and have been studied mainly in lab dishes, not in people.
Purple buds get their color from anthocyanins, shaped by genetics and cool temperatures, not by potency.
Michigan labels list THC and CBD content, not flavonoids.
body:
Cannabis flavonoids are plant pigments and protective compounds from the same family you'll find in berries, onions and tea. Researchers have identified more than 20 in cannabis, including three cannflavins found almost nowhere else. In the plant, they help with color and with handling stress. What they do in people is still largely unstudied, so here's the science without the hype.

## What Flavonoids Are

Flavonoids are polyphenols, a large family of natural compounds built on phenol rings. A 2016 overview counted about 6,000 of them. They turn up in fruits, vegetables, grains, bark, roots, stems, flowers, tea and wine, which is why nutrition researchers call many of them dietary flavonoids. They fall into subgroups, and three matter most for cannabis: flavones, flavonols and anthocyanins.

## Flavonoids in Cannabis: How Many and Where

The tally so far tops 20, and most are flavones and flavonols, in both free and sugar-bound forms. They appear in seedlings, leaves and flowers, but researchers haven't detected them in roots or seeds.

Amounts shift with growing conditions. Cannflavin A levels depend on a plant's genetics plus temperature, sunlight, rainfall and humidity. In one study, genetically identical clones grown at higher elevations made more cannflavins.

## What Flavonoids Do for the Plant

Plants make flavonoids for their own benefit. Across the plant world, these compounds:

- color flowers and fruits, which helps attract pollinators
- work as natural UV filters
- help defend against microbes and insects
- help plants cope with cold, drought and heat

## The Main Cannabis Flavonoids

| Flavonoid | Group | What stands out in cannabis |
|---|---|---|
| Apigenin | Flavone | One of the main flavones found in the plant |
| Luteolin | Flavone | The starting material the plant uses to build cannflavins A and B |
| Kaempferol | Flavonol | Present in free and sugar-bound forms |
| Quercetin | Flavonol | Present in free and sugar-bound forms |
| Cannflavins A, B and C | Prenylated or geranylated flavones | Almost unique to cannabis; cannflavin C was isolated from a high-THC plant |

Cannflavins were first isolated in the 1980s from a cannabis extract with the cannabinoids removed. In 2019, scientists at the University of Guelph identified two enzymes the plant uses to turn luteolin into cannflavins A and B. That finding opens a route to making them in yeast or bacteria instead of extracting tiny amounts from plants. Cannflavin A isn't strictly exclusive to cannabis, either; it has also been found in a species of monkeyflower.

## What Lab Research Is Exploring, and Its Limits

Most of the interest centers on inflammation. In early experiments, cannflavins reduced production of prostaglandin E2, an inflammation signaling molecule, in human cells grown in a dish. Later enzyme studies found that cannflavins A and B block two enzymes that make inflammation signals, one for PGE2 and one for leukotrienes. Other early work has looked at nerve cells in culture, parasites and computer models of viral proteins.

Those are cell, enzyme and computer studies, not trials in people. There's no human evidence that the flavonoids in cannabis flower or extracts change anything in the body, and the authors of a 2021 review call for clinical studies to find out. Research also lagged for decades because of cannabis's legal status. So think of flavonoids as interesting chemistry, not a reason to pick one product over another. If you have questions about a health condition, talk with your doctor.

## Flavonoids vs. Terpenes

Terpenes and flavonoids often get mentioned together, but they do different jobs. Terpenes are the plant's main aroma compounds, and more than 200 volatile compounds have been reported in cannabis. Flavonoids are polyphenols that work inside plant tissue, coloring and protecting it.

| | Flavonoids | Terpenes |
|---|---|---|
| What you notice | Color, in some cases | Aroma and flavor |
| Reported in cannabis | More than 20 | 58 monoterpenes and 38 sesquiterpenes, among 200-plus volatiles |
| Required on Michigan labels | No | No |

Researchers would like to know whether either group shapes the so-called [entourage effect](/blog/the-entourage-effect/), but that idea remains largely untested in people. For the aroma side of the story, see our [guide to cannabis terpenes](/blog/what-are-cannabis-terpenes/).

## Why Some Strains Turn Purple

Purple, red and blue tones come from anthocyanins, a flavonoid subgroup. In cannabis, the main purple pigment is cyanidin-3-rutinoside, also called keracyanin. Anthocyanins build up in the outer layers of leaves and flowers, where they help protect the plant from UV light, cold and other stress.

Color starts with genetics, since a plant has to carry the trait. Temperature can then bring it out. In a 2025 study of a cannabis line bred to turn purple, anthocyanin levels peaked when plants were held at 8 °C and 15 °C (about 46 °F and 59 °F). They dropped at colder and warmer settings. CBD content in that study followed plant maturity, not color. Color is about pigment; it isn't a potency reading.

## Why Flavonoids Rarely Appear on Labels

Michigan requires cannabis labels to show THC and CBD content, the testing lab, the harvest date where it applies, and required warnings. Flavonoids aren't on that list, so most packages never mention them. Terms like [full-spectrum](/blog/what-is-full-spectrum-cbd/) describe an extract that keeps more of the plant's compounds, not a measured flavonoid content. To compare products, start with the cannabinoid numbers; our guide to [cannabinoids](/blog/what-are-cannabinoids/) explains what they mean.

faq.q: Why do some buds turn purple?
faq.a: Mostly genetics, helped along by cool temperatures. The purple comes from anthocyanins, flavonoid pigments that build up in leaves and flowers; in cannabis the main one is cyanidin-3-rutinoside. Plants that carry the trait can deepen in color when grown cool; in one 2025 study, pigment peaked at steady temperatures of 8 °C and 15 °C. Purple does not signal higher potency, so check the THC and CBD numbers on the label.

They are flavonoids found almost only in cannabis. Cannflavins A, B and C are flavones with extra carbon side chains. A and B were first isolated in the 1980s; C was reported in 2008, from a high-THC plant. The plant builds A and B from luteolin, a common flavone. Lab studies have looked at how they affect inflammation-related enzymes in cells, but none of that research has been done in people yet.

faq.q: Do flavonoids change how cannabis feels?
faq.a: There is no evidence that they do. Research on cannabis flavonoids has been done in lab dishes and computer models, not in people. How cannabis feels depends mainly on the amount and mix of cannabinoids such as THC and CBD, plus your tolerance and setting. If you have questions about how cannabis might affect your health, talk with your doctor.

review.notes: Fact-check 2026-10-24: all five PMC/PubMed sources opened through NCBI E-utilities; the CRA rules PDF is the law-facts source for mi-labeling (michigan.gov refuses automated fetches, not re-opened). Fixed: the enzyme sentence (5-lipoxygenase makes leukotrienes, not PGE2); cannflavin C dates from 2008, not the 1980s; "cool nights" replaced with what the 2025 study measured; the 6,000 count dated to 2016; harvest date "where it applies". Six sources, all https and supporting.
review.writerNotes: Medical article: no shop, menu, deals or rewards links (the brief's closing shop link is dropped). Research described as in vitro/computational with limits; no anti-inflammatory, anticancer, heart or blood-sugar product claims; no advice to choose products for flavonoids. H1 uses the primary keyword exactly; the brief's "Flavor" in the H1 was replaced with "Chemistry" because the flavor role of cannabis flavonoids is not established by the sources.
